articles.title: TSE aceita ação contra Lula e Alckmin por desfile de escola de samba | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato alega abuso de poder político e econômico e uso indevido dos meios de comunicação; corregedor-eleitoral deu cinco dias para defesa dos investigados.
articles.summary: TSE aceita ação de Flávio Bolsonaro contra Lula e Alckmin por suposto abuso de poder e uso indevido de mídia em desfile de escola de samba de Niterói.
articles.body:
Acadêmicos de Niterói homenageou Lula no carnaval de 2026 — Foto: Leo Franco / AgNews

O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) decidiu aceitar uma ação de investigação judicial eleitoral contra o presidente Lula (PT) e seu vice Geraldo Alckmin (PSB), candidatos à reeleição, por suposto abuso de poder político e econômico cometido durante o desfile da escola de samba Acadêmicos de Niterói em fevereiro deste ano, no carnaval do Rio. O desfile teve a história de Lula como enredo .

A ação foi admitida pelo corregedor-eleitoral, ministro Antonio Carlos Ferreira, na sexta-feira (18). A petição, apresentada pelo candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e seu vice Alfredo Gaspar (PL), também cita a primeira-dama Janja Lula da Silva, o candidato a deputado federal pelo PT Marcelo Freixo e o prefeito de Niterói, Rodrigo Neves, como investigados. Pela decisão do ministro, eles têm até cinco dias para apresentar defesa.

O g1 entrou em contato com a assessoria de campanha do PT, mas não obteve resposta. O texto será atualizado se o partido se manifestar.

❗Admitir uma ação de investigação eleitoral não significa que a campanha e os candidatos serão punidos, nem que o corregedor-eleitoral concorde ou discorde dos argumentos de quem iniciou o processo. Nessa etapa, não se discute o conteúdo da ação. É uma decisão técnica. Aceitar o processo significa que o ministro entendeu que os fatos apresentados se encaixam nos requisitos de admissibilidade. Alguns aspectos levados em consideração: quem propôs a ação, se há a indicação de provas e se os fatos narrados poderiam, em tese, configurar abuso de poder econômico ou político.

Esta não é a primeira ação de investigação judicial eleitoral admitida no TSE na disputa deste ano. Há 9 outros processos semelhantes já protocolados.

O partido Novo também questionou o desfile da Acadêmicos do Niterói, e a ação foi admitida pelo corregedo em agosto. Em sua defesa, Lula alegou que carnavais retratam figuras políticas, que ele apenas concordou com o uso de seu nome, que os repasses foram isonômicos entre as 12 escolas do Rio de Janeiro e que não havia gravidade, dada a distância até as eleições. Nesse caso, o ministro Antonio Carlos Ferreira aguarda manifestação do Novo.

Em outro caso, o PT entrou com ação contra Flávio Bolsonaro por sua participação na Festa do Peão de Boiadeiro de Barretos, em agosto. O partido sustenta que houve financiamento empresarial indireto de campanha, já que o evento era patrocinado por empresas privadas, e que o tempo de palco cedido ao candidato sem contrapartida financeira configuraria como doação indireta de empresas, prática proibida pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). O corregedor também aprovou a admissibilidade deste processo em decisão publicada em 7 de setembro.

Márcio Nogueira, presidente da OAB de Rondônia e especialista em Direito Eleitoral e Digital, diz que esse tipo de processo é um dos instrumentos "mais severos de responsabilização na Justiça Eleitoral". O especialista explica que, se avançar, uma investigação judicial eleitoral pode levar à cassação do registro de candidatura ou do diploma do candidato, se ele for eleito, além de deixá-lo inelegível por oito anos.

Nogueira afirma que essa ação é utilizada para apurar abuso de poder econômico, abuso de poder político ou de autoridade e uso indevido dos meios de comunicação que, pela gravidade, comprometam a normalidade e a legitimidade da eleição. Investigações desta natureza estão contempladas no artigo 22 da Lei Complementar 64, de 1990.

Uma ação de investigação judicial não é a mesma coisa que uma representação eleitoral, classe de processo que o TSE tem recebido aos montes em 2026.

"AIJE é voltada à apuração de abuso de poder, exigindo a demonstração da gravidade da conduta e podendo resultar em cassação e inelegibilidade", afirma o presidente da OAB de Rondônia. "Já as representações eleitorais são utilizadas para apurar infrações específicas previstas na legislação, como propaganda irregular ou determinadas condutas vedadas, e as consequências dependem de cada infração, podendo envolver, por exemplo, multa ou cassação."

As duas condenações no TSE que deixaram Jair Bolsonaro inelegível até 2030 ocorreram em ações de investigação judicial eleitoral. A primeira tratou da reunião no Palácio da Alvorada com embaixadores estrangeiros, em julho de 2022 . No segundo caso, Bolsonaro foi condenado por abuso de poder político e econômico nas comemorações do Bicentenário da Independência , realizadas no dia 7 de setembro de 2022, em Brasília (DF) e no Rio de Janeiro (RJ).

O que dizem Flávio Bolsonaro e Alfredo Gaspar

Na petição contra Lula, os adversários argumentam que o abuso de poder econômico ocorreu porque, segundo eles, os municípios do Rio de Janeiro e de Niterói, o estado do Rio de Janeiro e a Embratur destinaram R$ 9,6 milhões à escola de samba, que ficou em último lugar e foi rebaixada .

Ainda de acordo com Flávio e seu vice, os repasses teriam ocorrido depois do anúncio do enredo, em julho de 2025. Além disso, haveria receitas privadas ainda não esclarecidas, possivelmente de empresas com contratos públicos e sem histórico de patrocinar escolas de samba.

Os candidatos também afirmam que houve uso indevido dos meios de comunicação social. Sustentam que o desfile foi transmitido em rede nacional de televisão aberta por cerca de 79 minutos e que a gravação continuou disponível em plataformas digitais. Segundo eles, essa exposição teria escapado ao regime jurídico da propaganda eleitoral.

No documento, pedem a produção de provas de diversos órgãos e entidades públicas e particulares, além de depoimentos de Janja, Marcelo Freixo e Rodrigo Neves. Solicitam também que, se reconhecido o abuso de poder político e econômico e uso indevido dos meios de comunicação, Lula e Alckmin sejam cassados e declarados inelegíveis.

Lula na Marquês de Sapucaí, no Rio. — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

articles.title: Lula e Flávio fazem comícios simultâneos em SC, reduto do bolsonarismo | G1
articles.standfirst: Em Florianópolis, atual presidente prometeu acabar com as bets. Em Joinville, senador disse que reajuste do Bolsa Família foi tentativa de comprar voto.
articles.summary: Em Florianópolis, atual presidente prometeu acabar com as bets. Em Joinville, senador disse que reajuste do Bolsa Família foi tentativa de comprar voto.
articles.body:
Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) fizeram comícios simultâneos em Santa Catarina neste sábado (19) — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), candidatos à Presidência, fizeram campanha em Santa Catarina neste sábado (19).

O estado é um reduto bolsonarista: em 2022, o então candidato à reeleição Jair Bolsonaro (PL) obteve por lá 69% dos votos no 2º turno contra Lula.

Na última pesquisa Quaest para presidente em Santa Catarina, divulgada em 24 de agosto, Flávio Bolsonaro tinha 45% das intenções de voto e Lula, 20%. Foram ouvidas 804 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 20 e 23 de agosto. A margem de erro é de 3 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%.

Já no cenário nacional, segundo a pesquisa Datafolha divulgada na quinta-feira (17), Lula tem 39% das intenções de voto no 1º turno, e Flávio Bolsonaro, 36%. Os dois estão tecnicamente empatados, dentro do intervalo da margem de erro de 2 pontos percentuais.

Lula critica Flávio e promete acabar com as bets

Lula fez um comício em Florianópolis, seu primeiro ato de campanha no estado neste ano. Em discurso, criticou a carta em que times de futebol pedem que as apostas continuem autorizadas no país e se posicionou contra as bets, dizendo considerar um dos motivos para o endividamento da população.

"Tomei uma decisão. Se depender da minha vontade, vou conversar com meu pessoal [do Ministério da] Fazenda, meu pessoal do BC [Banco Central], mas a verdade é que eu quero acabar com as bets", disse.

➡️ Alguns dos principais clubes brasileiros defenderam o mercado regulado de apostas no país em um manifesto publicado nas redes sociais na quinta-feira. O texto diz que, se as bets forem proibidas, "o futebol é que acaba".

Lula também criticou Flávio Bolsonaro, ainda que sem citá-lo diretamente. O presidente afirmou que o adversário quer vencer a eleição para tirar o pai da cadeia. "A ideia do outro [Flávio Bolsonaro]: 'Eu quero ganhar as eleições para tirar meu pai da cadeia'. E eu quero ganhar para manter ele na cadeia", afirmou.

Participaram do comício os candidatos da chapa petista no estado: Gelson Merisio (PSB), que tenta o cargo de governador, e Afrânio Boppré (PSOL) e Décio Lima (PT), que concorrem ao Senado.

Flávio acusa Lula de tentar comprar voto

Já o senador Flávio Bolsonaro participou, pela manhã, de um comício em Joinville, no norte de Santa Catarina.

O candidato afirmou que Lula tentou comprar o voto dos mais pobres ao assinar o decreto que reajustou o Bolsa Família em 15%.

"Ele [Lula] foi e tentou comprar o voto dos mais pobres, dando R$ 90 de reajuste para o Bolsa Família. Que vergonha, Lula, que vergonha. O Bolsonaro triplicou, deu mais R$ 420 do que era a média do Bolsa Família; você deu R$ 90", afirmou.

➡️ O reajuste foi anunciado na quinta-feira (17) e eleva o piso do programa de R$ 600 para R$ 691. Segundo o Ministério do Planejamento, o custo neste ano será de R$ 5,8 bilhões; para 2027, o impacto nas despesas será de R$ 22,7 bilhões.

Flávio também prometeu levar a questão do licenciamento ambiental para a Presidência, ao dizer que uma "burocracia danada" trava empreendimentos no Brasil.

Participaram do evento dois irmãos de Flávio: Carlos Bolsonaro (PL), candidato ao Senado, e Jair Renan (PL), que disputa uma vaga de deputado federal. Completam a chapa do PL no estado Jorginho Mello (PL), candidato ao governo, e Caroline de Toni (PL), também ao Senado.

Na última pesquisa Quaest com as intenções de voto em Santa Catarina, em 24 de agosto, Jorginho Mello (PL) tinha 50%; João Rodrigues (PSD), 17%; e Gelson Merísio (PSB), 4%.

A pesquisa ouviu 804 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 20 e 23 de agosto. A margem de erro é de 3 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa foi registrada no TSE sob o número SC-00517/2026 e BR-07160/2026.

articles.title: Mendonça e Fux pedem auxílio da PF para acessar celular de Vorcaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministros do STF receberam cópias de todo o material apreendido em celular do ex-dono do Banco Master. Eles cogitaram problemas operacionais para analisar os dados ou defeito na mídia entregue pela polícia.
articles.summary: Os ministros do STF solicitaram ajuda técnica após dificuldades para acessar o conteúdo do celular de Daniel Vorcaro, apreendido na Operação Compliance Zero.
articles.body:
Os ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) André Mendonça e Luiz Fux enviaram ofícios à Polícia Federal , neste sábado (19), afirmando que não conseguiram acessar o conteúdo do celular do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do Banco Master.

Nos ofícios, Mendonça e Fux pediram auxílio técnico da PF para conseguir analisar os dados .

Cópias do celular apreendido com Vorcaro na Operação Compliance Zero, que investiga fraudes do Master, foram disponibilizadas pela PF aos gabinetes dos ministros Mendonça, Cristiano Zanin, Flávio Dino, Alexandre de Moraes, Luiz Fux e Kassio Nunes Marques.

Os magistrados solicitaram o acesso ao material, que tem cerca de 500 gigabytes (GB) . Para se ter ideia, esse tamanho comportaria em torno de 140 mil imagens em alta resolução, mais de 120 mil arquivos de áudio em formato MP3 e cerca de 40 horas de filmes em alta resolução.

Nos ofícios à PF, Mendonça e Fux afirmaram que, até este sábado, não haviam conseguido analisar o material que estava no celular de Vorcaro, seja por dificuldades de ordem técnica ou por algum defeito contido nas mídias entregues pelos policiais .

Fachada do Banco Master, em São Paulo — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Segundo relatos feitos ao g1 , os dados do celular de Vorcaro estão divididos em pastas com chats, áudios e logs (registros de atividades feitas no aparelho).

Os dados extraídos foram organizados pela PF utilizando um software para perícia chamado IPED (Indexador e Processador de Evidências Digitais), que organiza e permite analisar o material coletado.

🔎 Esse programa facilita a navegação, permitindo buscas por palavras-chave, em conversas e documentos.

A PF usou ferramentas para acessar dados apagados ou protegidos por senha. Peritos da polícia utilizaram softwares especializados para copiar o conteúdo completo do aparelho, recuperar fragmentos de dados e rastrear registros de envio de mensagens e arquivos.

articles.title: Lawsuit accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, Google of AI pacing ‘collusion’
articles.summary: AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, Space XAI and Google are being sued over alleged collusion as pressure mounts to slow the rapid development of AI. The compla...
articles.body:
AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, Space XAI and Google are being sued over alleged collusion as pressure mounts to slow the rapid development of AI.

The complaint , filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for "industry-wide coordination" to "pace the frontier" as concerns mount over the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI.

"We must slow the space in which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote in a Sept. 12 essay.

The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating federal antitrust law.

Within hours of Amodei publishing his essay, Musk responded, saying "Dario is right," while Altman also said he agreed with Amodei. Hassabis called the proposal "the right path forward," according to the complaint.

Nick Rowley, one of the attorneys who filed the lawsuit on behalf of four plaintiffs, said decisions about AI safeguards should be made through government action rather than private agreements among major technology companies.

Rowley said in a statement to Politico that the case was filed to ensure "private self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful 'for profit' technology companies" don't result in AI "quickly spin[ing] out of human control."

"Humanity deserves iron clad safeguards when it comes to extinction event threats such as nuclear warfare and now the biggest risk to mankind in history," Rowley continued. "The rule of law should be established transparently and lawfully by our government, with accountability to the public."

The plaintiffs include Florida attorneys Charles Buist and Nick Spetsas, Cheyenne Hunt — an attorney who played a key role in exposing the sexual misconduct allegations against former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) — and California resident Christine Bullock.

Amodei's proposal had already raised antitrust concerns among lawmakers in Washington, after the Anthropic CEO suggested the government could provide a "narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations" so AI companies could work together on standards without violating U.S. antitrust law.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) rejected the idea during a Senate hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday.

"There is absolutely no world in which I will consent to giving the most powerful companies in the history of the world — a small group of three or four of them — antitrust exemptions so they can what … collude together?" Hawley said. "Absolutely no way that's happening."

articles.title: ‘It will never be the same’: How Trump turned on the Kennedy Center and brought it to its knees
articles.summary: Nine months from the day when cranes first placed Trump’s name on the marble façade, the institution has been brought to the brink
articles.body:
When President Donald Trump's name was ordered removed from the Kennedy Center this spring, it seemed that an opening to move on from his reign over the performing arts center might have emerged.

"I have instructed the Department of Commerce to make all necessary arrangements with Congress to allow a full and complete transfer of this Institution, giving them the responsibility for its Operation, Maintenance, and Management," the president wrote in a late-May Truth Social post , seemingly relinquishing the control he'd seized a year prior.

Speculation even bubbled up among some of the more than a dozen "ex-officio," board members — who don't get a vote but are not allied with Trump — over whether the former board chairman, billionaire philanthropist David Rubenstein, could be brought back to help restore the center's fundraising and programming, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. (CNN has asked Rubenstein for comment.)

But after Trump said he would remain chairman, "it kind of all squelched pretty quickly," one of the sources said. The hope that his crusade to rename a monument dedicated to the memory of John F. Kennedy had ended turned out to be wishful thinking.

Instead, nine months from a cold December day when cranes first placed Trump's name on the marble façade, the institution has been brought to the brink by the president still very much engaged in a fight: lights have been turned off inside , infrastructure is crumbling and protests swirl while legal battles mount.

A lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex-officio board member, led to a judge's ruling that Trump's name had to be scraped off the building and that the board could not shut down the facility altogether.

Trump has only ratcheted up his threats to tear down the building in response to the legal setbacks: The president was seen with a poster this week through the window of Air Force One that appeared to read "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." Though the federal judge has since ordered a 30-day notice be given before any major change happens, it's not at all clear where things go from here.

Late Friday night, the administration argued in court that the Kennedy Center must close for two years, asking the federal judge in the case to allow it so that the "dangerously dilapidated and decrepit" building can be renovated.

On the same day, over a dozen Kennedy Center employees were laid off, including its lead spokesperson, according to two sources familiar with the matter — gutting an already skeleton staff. The Kennedy Center declined to comment on the cuts.

Trump has said previous leadership is to blame for the dire financial situation. During a contentious board call this week, he also blamed Beatty for bringing litigation that, he said, has contributed to the center's downfall.

While the president and his allies on the board argue his name needs to be re-affixed to the building to revive fundraising, current and former officials, performers and industry officials say it is precisely Trump's involvement that alienated the center's donors and prompted scores of artists to cancel their performances.

"The Broadway productions will not come back, the artists will not come back," said a source familiar with discussions about programming. "None of those donors will come back as long as Donald J Trump is the chairman."

Current and former Kennedy Center officials, musicians, artists and other performers with ties to the center suggest that Trump's takeover has added a permanent imprint on the Kennedy Center, whether or not his name ultimately ends up on the building.

"There are wonderful theaters throughout this country, and they are certainly part of the cultural ecology," said LaRue Allen, president and executive director of the Martha Graham Dance Company, which has a 50-year history with the institution. "But the Kennedy Center — it is our nation's capital. It is our national showcase."

Another Kennedy Center source who recently left said simply: "It will never be the same."

CNN has asked the White House for comment.

'The Kennedy Center, they do a beautiful job, an incredible job'

Trump's focus on the Kennedy Center is emblematic of a notable shift from his first administration to a second one that has targeted arts, cultural and educational pillars across the country, in addition to Trump's unrelenting desire to remake the nation's capital to his liking.

In his first term, Trump mostly avoided the venue, skipping the Kennedy Center Honors after awardees threatened to boycott the event if he attended. The White House even said in a 2017 statement that the president and First Lady Melania Trump were not participating "to allow the honorees to celebrate without any political distraction."

And when the Kennedy Center initially received $25 million in funding in a March 2020 Covid stimulus package, Trump defended the aid, saying: "The Kennedy Center, they do a beautiful job, an incredible job."

Nine months later, however, he singled out a $40 million line-item for the center while criticizing a subsequent December 2020 Covid aid bill — a foreshadowing of his future disaffection.

By his 2024 campaign, Trump made clear that going after so-called "wokeism" would be a pillar of a second presidency. He didn't appear to single out the Kennedy Center on the campaign trail, but in his third week in office he'd already set a takeover plan in motion.

"At my direction, we are going to make the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C., GREAT AGAIN, " Trump wrote on Truth Social in February 2025.

Trump said he had fired Rubenstein as chairman of the board as well as board trustees "who do not share our Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture."

The takeover became the first domino in a cascade of Trump moves to remake the nation's capital, including the demolition of the East Wing of the White House, the closure and remodeling of the busiest public golf course in Washington, DC, and his ongoing efforts to build a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery — projects all still being fought over in court.

Though Trump has widely criticized cultural institutions and museums, he's been able to exert only so much control over them, primarily by reducing their federal funding. The federal government has gutted the agencies that fund the arts, including the National Endowment for the Arts and National Endowment for the Humanities, and denied and rescinded tens of millions of dollars in grants to organizations that don't align with the president's values.

But the Kennedy Center is one of the few cultural institutions where the president has been able to flex more of his power by seizing control of the board. He has similarly tried to bring the federally funded Smithsonian Institution to heel, with more uneven results.

A week after Trump's board takeover, the president was named as its chairman, and he installed longtime loyalist Richard Grenell as executive director.

"So we took over the Kennedy Center," Trump told reporters. "I'm going to be chairman of it, and we're going to make sure that it's good and it's not going to be woke. There's no more woke in this country."

His new role prompted several cancellations, including most notably the Broadway show "Hamilton."

Leading up to the center's Kennedy Center Honors in December 2025, which Trump himself was hosting, the president began referring to the building as the "Trump Kennedy Center."

On December 18, 2025, the board made that declaration official by voting to rename the facility the "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," saying that the change honored Trump's work at the center after taking over.

One day later, new signage was installed to add Trump's name to the building's façade.

The legal battle and wave of cancellations that has ensued present particular challenges for an institution that makes part of its budget from ticket sales.

Operating as a non-profit, the Kennedy Center received roughly $37 million from Congress in the last fiscal year, according to the latest appropriations legislation signed into law. But the bulk of its revenue comes from programming and private donations. In fiscal year 2024, during the Biden administration, the Kennedy Center reported $307 million in revenues, according to documents filed with the IRS.

Last year, Grenell sought to revamp the center's calendar to include, in his words, more family-friendly programming. He brought in "Dog Man: The Musical," based on the popular kids' graphic novel series, at the recommendation of second lady Usha Vance.

At the same time, the center became a place to host events that lean in to Trumpian ties, including the premiere of the documentary "Melania," a Charlie Kirk memorial and the FIFA World Cup draw (where the organization gave Trump a peace prize).

But after Trump's name was added to the building, a wave of performers pulled out, and ticket sales sagged. Multiple sources told CNN earlier this year that attendance at the Kennedy Center had been so low that for months it had to "paper the house" — a theater term that means to fill seats by offering free or discounted tickets.

"There was a haze of despair around the performances. Nobody was showing up to performances," Carlos Simon, the Kennedy Center composer-in-residence since 2021, told CNN.

Simon, who is in the last year of his residence, noted that the National Symphony Orchestra is now playing at other venues in Washington. He said he's stayed in his role at the Kennedy Center "for the morale of the folks who were still there trying to do the good work of presenting music."

"I feel really bad that it's become this political tool or pawn, but music still has to go on," he said.

Amid the cancellations, Trump announced in February that the Kennedy Center would close for two years on July 4 to allow for renovations — a move critics suspected was to being made more to provide cover for the shrinking pool of patrons than because of the need for such a dramatic closure.

The Kennedy Center also received an influx of funding last year thanks to Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," which contained $257 million for the center to pursue "necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures."

Yet the board has argued only Trump's help can muster the funds to renovate the building — and Trump has made clear his help will only come with naming rights.

In the meantime, Matt Floca, Grenell's successor as executive director, this week told the judge in the Beatty case that the center needs to temporarily close due to safety concerns.

Even if the building survives, officials say getting the center's programming to return — particularly Broadway shows — would still take months if not several years.

That is under the assumption, of course, that performances would be willing to return, said the source involved in the center's programming.

"If we started now in terms of engaging with property companies, going back and forth and getting a deal made, we could have Broadway tours back at the Kennedy Center by the basically middle of '27 into '28," the source said. "That's how long it takes for all these pieces to be put in place."

CNN's Katelyn Polantz contributed to this report.

articles.title: The 2026 midterms are six weeks away. Which party has a better chance of winning? Here's what the latest polls say.
articles.summary: The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear trends are emerging.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are just 60 days away. Most of the key primaries have been decided . With Labor Day weekend behind us, the fall campaign is now underway.

So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to zoom out … and geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. And 60 days can be an eternity in politics.

Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans and Democrats were statistically tied on the generic ballot. Two months later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House .

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 8.9 points on the generic ballot. Two months later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House .

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by Election Day, voters had broken against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House ; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively .

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot: about 6 or 7 percentage points , on average . They probably won't reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is possible — but Dems are also playing defense in places like Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire. Here are the 10 races to follow:

What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 3 to 8 percentage points .

Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress)

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director)

What the latest polls say : For the last month or so, El-Sayed has consistently led Rogers by anywhere from 1 to 7 percentage points .

What the latest polls say : Every poll conducted since July shows Brown leading Husted , with margins ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points.

Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with the two most recent polls putting him ahead by 8 to 9 percentage points .

Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman)

Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu, who both won their Sept. 8 primaries, have traded leads in recent polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Peltola has led Sullivan in all but one statewide poll — a late June New York Times/Siena survey put Sullivan 2 points ahead. Surveys conducted since Alaska's Aug. 18 primary have given her a slim lead .

Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress)

Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete)

What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries. But the most recent polling tends to favor Hinson by 2 to 5 percentage points.

Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general)

Democrat James Talarico (state legislator)

What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted over the summer has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 2 and 6 points.

Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor)

Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support)

What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent results suggest Osborn could be competitive.

Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 58% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 39% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at nearly 20%.

Again, history can provide perspective . In June 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70.5% disapprove and 24.4% approve. That's a 46-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

articles.title: Trump ramps up feud with press after week of setbacks
articles.summary: An embattled Trump has injected his fight with the news media with new acrimony, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has infused his ongoing feud with the White House press with a new level of acrimony.

Journalists from three major media outlets - CNN, Politico and MS Now - were denied access and had their press credentials confiscated on Saturday morning as they attempted to enter the White House grounds for work.

As media watchdog organisations and the White House Correspondents Association cry foul, Trump appears set to press ahead with a sweeping effort to punish these outlets.

In his Truth Social post announcing his decision on Friday, he said he was "banning" the organisations because "of their constant 'reporting' of fake news". In remarks later that day, he complained that "something is wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories".

"If they want to write them, that's fine," he continued. "I don't have to let them into the people's house", he said, referring to the White House.

Journalists denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets

The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.

First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".

These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.

His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions.

The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.

Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.

In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka – a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.

Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.

The White House bans, however, represent a dramatic escalation.

The restrictions include access to the entirety of the White House grounds, not just the press pool. And they target entire news organisations, not just a single disfavoured correspondent.

While Trump has been clear about the motives behind his decision, he has shed little light on why he has acted now. He has regularly criticised his press coverage since he first entered national politics more than a decade ago, but he said on Friday there was no specific incident that prompted his announcement.

At the moment, however, the president is embattled.

Even beyond the week of clear setbacks, he is in the midst of an unpopular and difficult-to-resolve war of choice in Iran, which has led to a surge in energy and other consumer prices, deflating his standing with the American public.

Polls also suggest his party faces an uphill battle to retain control of the House of Representatives and perhaps the Senate in November's crucial midterm congressional elections.

His attempts to improve the public's mood by touting his accomplishments in campaign events and at his Republican Party's convention earlier this month in Texas have, at least so far, proven ineffective.

There may be more behind Trump's decision to lash out at the media this weekend. But it could also simply be an indication of presidential frustration in the face of events and circumstances, some of his own making, that are turning against him.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

articles.title: Security expert hails Trump's Greenland pact as a 'big deal' on par with Alaska purchase
articles.summary: Col. Grant Newsham says President Donald Trump's Greenland deal effectively neutralizes Russian and Chinese ambitions across North American geography.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's newly announced security agreement with Denmark and Greenland would block U.S. adversaries from establishing bases in Greenland and limit adversarial investments on the island, a move one security expert says limits China and Russia's ambitions in the region. Speaking on "Fox & Friends Weekend," Center for Security Policy senior fellow and retired U.S. Marine Col. Grant Newsham compared Trump's pact with Denmark and Greenland to the U.S. acquisition of Alaska in 1867. Newsham argued the agreement secures vital North American defense geography while limiting Russian and Chinese expansion. "This is a big deal. This is right up there with Secretary of State Seward getting Alaska," Newsham said Saturday. RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS "It's a little different, because we haven't bought the place, but it locks up or brings into the fold, really, key terrain, key geography, up on our northeast," he explained. "Russia and the Chinese, in particular, they can't get in there militarily, and they cannot get in economically." On Friday, the president announced the deal in a post on Truth Social, saying the agreement would give the U.S. permanent control over security in Greenland. "I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns," Trump wrote. "There will be NO COST to the United States! At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," he added. DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY Denmark and Greenland have emphasized that the agreement, which requires formal signatures and parliamentary procedures before taking effect, will preserve their "sovereignty and territorial integrity." RUBIO WARNS CHINA AFTER PANAMA SHIP DETENTIONS, CALLS HEMISPHERE SOVEREIGNTY 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' Newsham compared the move to Trump's previous foreign policy decisions, arguing the Greenland agreement fits what he sees as a broader strategy to defend the U.S. homeland. "Look at how the Chinese have been rolled back in Panama. And look what President Trump has done with Venezuela. You can see that there's a plan here for defending our homeland. And this really is a big deal, to put it in simple terms," Newsham said. TRUMP ENVOY WARNS CHINA'S POWER MOVE AT SEA IS THREAT 'WE CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE' Newsham said he believes the agreement gives Washington the freedom it needs to keep adversaries out of Greenland, though he predicted China and Russia would voice opposition. "They'll complain. They won't like it, but there's not much they can do about it," Newsham said. "They'll probably step up their activities in the territories they have up there. But nonetheless, this is a huge advance for the United States and our position." GREENLAND TALKS ON ‘GOOD TRAJECTORY,’ WHITE HOUSE SAYS AMID TRUMP TAKEOVER PUSH Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also highlighted the president's plans to expand the U.S. military presence in Greenland, reposting part of Trump's statement: "We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised the Greenland agreement, writing on X, "This historic deal is a huge win for the United States and the American people. Thanks to President Trump's vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the U.S. taxpayer." "Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area. This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," Rubio added.

articles.title: LA homelessness fraud cases expose deeper problem than stolen millions, oversight hawk warns
articles.summary: Rep. Michael Cloud says Los Angeles homelessness fraud cases expose a funding system that rewards program managers while keeping people in dependency.
articles.body: Federal charges alleging that millions of dollars were siphoned from Los Angeles homelessness programs are exposing what one lawmaker told Fox News Digital is a deeper failure in the way Washington funds and measures such programs. The latest cases out of Los Angeles fuel the concern of Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas that only are corrupt providers stealing taxpayer money, but that the programs aren't meeting their goal of getting people off the streets. "The only people really getting upward mobility in these programs, it would seem, is the people running the programs," Cloud told Fox News Digital after a House Oversight hearing examining federally funded homelessness programs in Los Angeles, Seattle and elsewhere. "And that’s not really what the program’s supposed to be about." LA REAL ESTATE VET COMES AT MAYOR BASS WITH RECEIPTS OVER DAMNING HOMELESSNESS REPORT: 'SHE DOESN'T GET IT' Federal prosecutors charged three defendants Wednesday in separate homelessness-fraud cases involving alleged misuse of taxpayer funds, including money allegedly spent on a nightclub and adjacent bingo hall and bribes allegedly tied to fake housing referrals. Los Angeles’ homelessness agency paid one of the suspect nonprofits more than $75 million, according to federal prosecutors, leading Cloud to seek out the real culprits blazing the money trail. WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE Cloud said the fraud itself is only one piece of a broader problem, and that the system appears to reward spending and program activity without adequately measuring lasting outcomes. Government too often judges success by "how much money we send out the door" instead of whether the spending is "actually helping people" or whether safeguards are in place to ensure taxpayer dollars are being used properly, Cloud said – describing the system as having been "incentivized for fraud." "We’ve got to take those incentives out and get back to making sure that all these programs have incentives for oversight and that the dollars are managed well," Cloud said. LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS Some programs can keep a person "kind of in a cycle of dependency so that the program manager has job security, in a sense, and gets to live off the government dime," Cloud said "You [are seeing] as we begin to look into waste, fraud and abuse, why is it that these Democrat-led states are saying, no, we don't want the controls in place," he said, pointing to Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass’ decision to step down from the LAHSA commission. Los Angeles is not alone, he said, citing what has been called the feds’ "Housing First" philosophy – generally prioritizing placing homeless in housing with less immediate regard for sobriety, mental-health treatment or overall stabilizing services. WATCH: DR. OZ SAYS NEWSOM, OTHER BLUE STATES HAVE TURNED MEDICAID FRAUD INTO A 'FEATURE' Cloud did not use the term "Housing First" during the interview, but he described the concern behind that critique, arguing that some homelessness programs define success in ways that leave people dependent on government rather than moving toward independence. Housing First is distinct from HUD’s "Continuum of Care" framework, which is the local funding and coordination structure through which nonprofit providers, state and local governments and other organizations receive federal homelessness money. WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES In Los Angeles, LAHSA leads the local Continuum of Care, which HUD says received nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars over the previous five years. Under Secretary Scott Turner, HUD moved to suspend LAHSA this year, citing alleged failures involving financial management, internal controls and safeguards against conflicts of interest. LAHSA has challenged the federal action in court. "The ‘housing first’ experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results," Turner said in June when HUD announced a $4.04 billion Continuum of Care funding opportunity. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "This ideology promised to end homelessness. Instead, billions of taxpayer dollars were spent while homelessness increased to record levels." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That funding will focus on organizations aiding treatment and recovery, while setting aside $1.3 billion for new projects prioritizing transitional housing and supportive services and adding measures intended to prevent fraud, waste and abuse.

articles.title: Trump announces new 'AI Force,' vows to protect industry as AI czar announcement nears
articles.summary: Trump's new AI Force mirrors his first-term Space Force creation, with a high-IQ "czar" appointment coming soon to oversee the booming industry.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he is creating an "AI Force" and plans to name an artificial intelligence czar as his administration pushes to accelerate the growth of AI in the U.S. Trump said in a lengthy Truth Social post that his administration would resist efforts to restrict the rapidly developing technology while using the existing criminal and civil justice systems to address potential wrongdoing. "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the post read. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" GOP LAWMAKERS SMELL SOMETHING ELSE BEHIND BIG TECH'S AI DOOMSDAY WARNINGS: 'SOMETHING ELSE GOING ON' Trump added that the government would also be "looking for BAD" and said existing criminal and civil laws could be used to address problems involving the technology. "For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," the president's post continued. "To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" Trump did not provide details about the structure, authority or membership of the proposed AI Force, or identify potential candidates to serve as its czar. POWERFUL COLD WAR-ERA TOOL TRUMP COULD USE IN AN AI EMERGENCY IS SET TO EXPIRE IN DECEMBER Trump's announcement comes as lawmakers grapple with whether and how to regulate the rapidly developing technology. Some Republicans have questioned calls for additional government oversight, while others have pushed for safeguards after AI industry leaders raised concerns about increasingly capable models. Earlier this week, Trump joined the debate by rejecting calls for additional government regulation of the industry, arguing that restrictions could hinder the U.S. in its competition with China. In Saturday’s post, Trump compared criticism of AI and data centers to several other political controversies and argued that opposition to data-center construction had largely failed. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS Trump also predicted that AI could eventually account for as much as 25% of U.S. gross domestic product, though he did not cite a source for the estimate. "AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP," he wrote. "We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a separate Truth Social post, Trump asked people to choose within the post on what to call AI. "Many people think that the words "Artificial Intelligence" are inaccurate, and very ineloquent, relative to AI, or Artificial Intelligence. A far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)," he wrote. "This is a Poll, and I would appreciate everybody voting! Which is the best name for this ever growing "Revolution?" President DONALD J. TRUMP"
